c.tagline: French colonial port on the world's second-largest natural bay, gateway to Madagascar's wild north.

taxi.fareNote: No ride-hailing apps operate here. Shared taxis-be (minibuses) run fixed routes across town for a few hundred ariary, while private taxis are unmetered — agree the fare before setting off.

emergency.note: Emergency response outside the main towns is very limited; carry a local SIM and keep your lodge's direct number handy.

avoid.reason: Avoid the port area and unlit streets anywhere in town after dark, as muggings occur.
Keep phones and jewelry out of sight in the market and along beaches, and use a trusted driver rather than walking at night.

hood_desc: The historic lower colonial town along the seafront and port, home to the Bazary Be market, faded French mansions, and the promenade over the great bay; the walkable heart for first-time visitors.
The lively main artery climbing through the upper town, lined with the city's best restaurants, bars, hotels, and tour operators; where evenings and nightlife concentrate.
A dense, workaday residential district set back from the water, with local markets and cheap eateries; authentic and inexpensive but short on sights.
A quieter residential and expat-leaning neighborhood on the town's outskirts near the old SCAMA estate; calm and green, better for longer stays with a car.

water.note: Drink bottled or treated water only.

transit.hours: Taxi-be run roughly 6:00 AM to 7:00 PM; after dark private taxis are the only option.
transit.note: Antsiranana has no formal bus, tram, or rail network. Shared taxis-be (minibuses) ply fixed routes across town, supplemented by private unmetered taxis.
transit.pay: Pay the taxi-be conductor in cash on board (a few hundred ariary per ride); private taxi fares are negotiated before departure. No transit cards exist.

bus: Shared taxi-be minibuses within the city
Taxi-brousse (long-distance bush taxis) to Ambanja, Ambilobe and beyond
ferry: Small boats to Ramena and around the bay

transit.m: Private taxi to the town centre (10-15 min)

tip.r: Not obligatory; rounding up or leaving 5-10% for good service in tourist restaurants is appreciated.

food.name: Grilled prawns and langouste
food.desc: Diego is famous for having Madagascar's best camarons; giant prawns and spiny lobster split, grilled over coals and served with garlic butter and rice.

places.name: Ramena beach restaurants
places.note: Simple shacks along the sand cooking the morning's catch to order with sea views.

places.name: Tsara Be

places.name: La Cantine
places.note: Rustic room doing both Malagasy and French dishes; strong on prawns and fish.

food.name: Poisson au coco
food.desc: Reef fish simmered in coconut milk with ginger, tomato and green mango - the coastal Antankarana way of cooking, quite unlike the highland kitchen.

places.name: Ramena beach restaurants
places.note: Coconut fish is the default order once you have picked your fish off the ice.

places.name: Saveurs de Diego Suarez
places.note: Local kitchen focused on Malagasy home cooking rather than tourist menus.

places.name: La Cantine
places.note: Coconut curries and stews served in generous, unfussy portions.

food.name: Romazava
food.desc: Madagascar's national dish: zebu beef stewed with brede mafana, the leaf that leaves your mouth tingling, plus ginger, tomato and a mountain of rice.

places.name: La Cantine
places.note: Its romazava is the dish reviewers mention first; hearty and properly made.

places.name: Saveurs de Diego Suarez
places.note: Everyday Malagasy plates at local prices, romazava included.

places.name: Bazary Be food stalls
places.note: Market hotely serve romazava and rice from mid-morning for a couple of dollars.

food.name: Masikita zebu skewers
food.desc: Small cubes of zebu threaded on sticks, grilled hard over charcoal and dipped in salt, chilli and lime; the classic evening street snack.

places.name: Rue Colbert evening grills

places.name: Bazary Be food stalls

places.name: Ramena beach restaurants
places.note: Skewers grilled on the beach alongside the fish, usually with coconut rice.

food.name: Zebu steak with green pepper
food.desc: Lean humped-cattle steak in a sauce of Malagasy green peppercorns or vanilla - the colonial-French side of Diego's cooking, and done well here.

places.name: Tsara Be
places.note: Reliable kitchen and the best-reviewed restaurant in town for a proper sit-down steak.

places.name: Le Grand Hotel Diego
places.note: The town's landmark hotel dining room; French-Malagasy menu and a colonial-era terrace.

places.name: La Cantine
places.note: Does the European half of its menu seriously, steaks included.

food.name: Mofo gasy and sambos
food.desc: Breakfast in the north: sweet rice-flour pancakes cooked in dimpled iron pans, and small fried samosas eaten hot from paper with sweet coffee.

places.name: Bazary Be market stalls
places.note: Pancake pans fire up at dawn; the cheapest and most authentic breakfast in Diego.

places.name: Rue Colbert morning carts
places.note: Carts sell mofo gasy, sambos and koba slices to office workers each morning.

places.name: Saveurs de Diego Suarez
places.note: Sit-down option for Malagasy snacks if you would rather not eat on the street.

food.name: Rhum arrange
food.desc: Local cane rum steeped for weeks with vanilla, lychee, ginger or wild honey; every bar keeps its own jars and pours a small glass after dinner.

places.name: Le Grand Hotel Diego
places.note: Bar with a long line of infusion jars; a comfortable place to try several.

places.name: Tsara Be
places.note: House infusions offered at the end of the meal, vanilla being the local signature.

places.name: Ramena beach restaurants
places.note: Beach bars pour punch coco and vanilla rum at sunset.

food.name: THB and fresh tropical juice
food.desc: Three Horses Beer is Madagascar's near-universal lager; alongside it, juices pressed from mango, tamarind, baobab or coconut water straight from the nut.

places.name: Bazary Be market juice stalls
places.note: Fresh-pressed seasonal juice and green coconuts opened while you wait.

places.name: Rue Colbert bars
places.note: The town's main strip of terraces; cold THB from late afternoon onward.

places.name: Ramena beach restaurants
places.note: Standard beach pairing: cold THB with a plate of grilled prawns.

landmarks: Mer d'Emeraude (Emerald Sea)
A dreamlike lagoon of impossibly green shallows beyond the bay's entrance, reached by pirogue for sandbank picnics and world-class snorkelling.
Les Trois Baies (Three Bays)
A wild coastal trilogy of Sakalava, Pigeon, and Dune bays, linked by walking trails past turquoise coves and kitesurf-perfect winds.
Montagne d'Ambre National Park
A rainforest island in the sky above the dry north, sheltering crater lakes, waterfalls, chameleons, and seven lemur species in misty highland forest.
Tsingy Rouge
A surreal scarlet forest of eroded laterite pinnacles hidden in a canyon south of the city, glowing crimson against green scrubland.
Nosy Lonjo (Sugarloaf)
The perfect cone islet rising from Antsiranana Bay, a sacred fady site and the unmistakable emblem of the world's second-largest bay.
Ramena Beach
The city's favourite escape, a golden fishing-village beach near the bay mouth where grilled seafood shacks face dhow-dotted turquoise water.
Rue Colbert and the Colonial Old Town
Diego Suarez's faded-grandeur main street, lined with creole verandas, art-deco relics, and the legendary Hotel de la Marine facade.
Cap Diego
A headland across the bay reached by ferry, pairing a historic French military outpost with sweeping panoramas over Antsiranana's vast natural harbour.
Baie de Sakalava
A crescent of white sand and steady trade winds ranked among the Indian Ocean's premier kitesurfing arenas, backed by baobabs and dunes.
Ankarana Special Reserve
A day-trip-worthy massif of grey tsingy limestone needles, bat-filled caves, and subterranean rivers roamed by crowned lemurs.

train.note: Madagascar's surviving passenger railways are all in the centre and southeast of the island - Fianarantsoa-Manakara, Antananarivo-Toamasina and the Antananarivo-Antsirabe line reopened in December 2023 - and none of them comes anywhere near the far north. The only rails ever laid around Antsiranana were narrow-gauge military and industrial lines built around 1900 and long since lifted. As an island nation, Madagascar has no international rail connections at all.

bus.note: Everything overland is by taxi-brousse (shared minibus) from the gare routiere: Antananarivo is roughly 1,100 km away via the RN4 and RN6 and takes 24-30 hours, usually with an overnight stop, while Ambanja (for the Nosy Be ferry) is 6-8 hours and Ambilobe 3-4 hours. Cotisse Transport (https://www.cotisse-transport.com/) is the most established branded operator and takes advance reservations; most other services are pay-at-the-station and leave only when full. Madagascar is an island, so no bus crosses a border, and the northern roads deteriorate badly in the cyclone season from January to March.

ferry.note: Antsiranana sits on one of the world's largest natural harbours and the port takes cargo ships and occasional cruise calls, but there is no scheduled passenger ferry in or out. Boats from the harbour and from Ramena beach are charter pirogues and dive craft heading for the Emerald Sea and Nosy Hara rather than transport services. To reach Nosy Be by sea you travel overland to Ankify near Ambanja, 6-8 hours away, and take the speedboat ferry from there. Cargo boats occasionally carry passengers towards the Comoros, but they are informal, uninsured and not recommended.

half.name: Montagne des Français
half.blurb: Hilltop overlooking the bay with colonial-era ruins, birdwatching, and rare baobab trees on the ascent.

half.name: Windsor Castle
half.blurb: Ruined colonial watchtower reached by a hike through dry forest and mangroves, with sweeping views over the strait.

full.name: Nosy Hara Marine Park
full.blurb: Protected archipelago of small limestone islands offshore, known for snorkeling and dramatic coastal scenery.
